# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about how we miss the world while living in it. Not in the grand, philosophical sense that gets written about in self-help books—though there's truth in that too—but in the smaller, more immediate way. The way we walk past the same coffee shop every morning for three years and never really see it. The way we use our phones to photograph sunsets instead of looking at them. The way our own hands, which we use thousands of times per day, remain basically strangers to us.

There's a cup on my desk right now. It's white, ceramic, with a small chip on the rim where I've carelessly clinked it against my teeth while drinking too hot coffee. Nothing remarkable about it. I've owned it for maybe four years. But if I actually stop and look at it—really look at it—there's something almost startling about its ordinariness. The way the light catches the glaze. The slight imperfections in the glazing that suggest human hands shaped it. The weight of it, designed perfectly to fit a hand that isn't mine, that doesn't exist, but that the potter imagined anyway.

Who made this cup? I have no idea. Somewhere in a factory or a studio, someone shaped clay. They did this thousands of times, probably. Their hands knew this motion the way my hands know how to type, unconsciously, automatically, until the motion becomes meditation. Maybe they were thinking about something else. Maybe they were happy. Maybe they were bored and wished they were doing anything other than shaping cups. Maybe it was Tuesday.

The cup is ordinary. The person who made it was ordinary. And yet there's something almost unbearably poignant about holding an object that represents that intersection of intention and accident, care and routine, the permanent and the temporary (that chip, evidence of my carelessness, will outlast me).

I think this is what I'm trying to understand: why does everything seem simultaneously profound and trivial? Why can't I decide if life is meaningful?

Maybe it's because both are true at once.

---

There's a tree outside my window. I'm sure I've never really looked at it before, but right now I'm looking at it, and I'm struck by how complicated it is. The branches don't follow any pattern I can discern, but they're not random either. Each branch seems to have a reason, a logic, a history of growth responding to light and gravity and wind. The bark is textured in a way that suggests time—years of weather, insects, disease, healing. Some of the branches are dead. Some are being slowly consumed by moss or lichen, those opportunistic organisms that wait for weakness and then move in, not maliciously, just pragmatically, taking what's available.

This tree doesn't know it's beautiful. It doesn't know anything, probably. It grows and exists and responds to stimuli, but there's no consciousness in there, no awareness of its own being. And yet I find myself moved by it. Why? What am I responding to? Am I projecting consciousness onto it, manufacturing meaning where there is none? Or is the beauty somehow independent of interpretation—inherent in the thing itself?

I think I've spent a lot of my life waiting for things to be big enough to matter. Big emotions, big events, big meanings. And I've missed most of the actual content of my existence in the process, which is composed almost entirely of small things. Small moments. Small observations. The particular way light falls through a window. The taste of a really good tomato. The surprising warmth of another person's hand.

When you think about it, everything is small. Even the things that seem big are composed of moments, which are small. An entire human lifetime is small in the span of geological time. The solar system is small in the galaxy. The galaxy is small in the universe. Everything keeps getting smaller the farther you zoom out, except it also keeps getting bigger the farther you zoom in. Every atom contains a solar system of smaller particles. Every second contains an infinity of smaller moments if you're willing to divide it infinitely.

So there's no scale that's actually meaningful. No level of magnification that's the "right" one. We're forced to choose arbitrarily, and the choice we make determines what we see.

---

I've been unemployed for three months. I left a job that was paying me well and that I was reasonably good at, but it felt like I was slowly being absorbed into an institution, losing the ability to distinguish between my own preferences and the preferences the institution had trained me to have. I couldn't remember if I actually liked anything anymore or if I'd just been conditioned to perform liking.

The first month was exhilarating. No alarm clock. Time stretched out luxuriously. I made ambitious plans. I would write! I would exercise! I would learn something new! I would become the person I always imagined I could be if I just had enough time.

The second month was less exhilarating. I was less productive than I'd thought I'd be. I was also less happy than I'd thought I'd be. Turns out unlimited free time doesn't automatically produce fulfillment. You still have to do something with it, and the something you do with it has to mean something to you, and that's actually pretty hard to figure out.

The third month—now—I'm in a strange place. I've accepted that I'm not going to magically become a different person. I'm the same person I was, just with less money and more time. But I'm also starting to see the time differently. It's not a resource to be optimized anymore. It's just what's happening. Hours pass. Some of them are boring. Some of them are interesting. Most of them are both, depending on how I'm looking at them.

I think the problem with how we normally talk about productivity and fulfillment is that we treat them as separate things—you're either productive (and therefore worthy) or you're not. But there's a whole category of time that's neither productive nor unproductive. It's just time. Sitting time. Looking-out-the-window time. Thinking-about-nothing-in-particular time. And that time, I'm realizing, might be important. Not important in the sense that it produces something valuable, but important in the sense that it's part of being alive.

---

I've been reading a lot about attention lately. How attention is the most valuable currency we have, and how everything in the modern world is designed to steal it. Social media companies employ hundreds of engineers specifically to figure out how to make their apps more addictive, how to hack into our psychology and redirect our attention toward their product. It's worked, obviously. We're all walking around in a state of mild distraction, constantly half-listening to conversations because part of our attention is always somewhere else, probably in our phones.

But here's what I'm wondering: is the solution to pay more attention? To cultivate mindfulness and presence? Or is that just another way to optimize yourself, to make yourself more efficient, to turn every moment into an opportunity for self-improvement?

I don't know. I think maybe the answer is just to look at things sometimes. Not with the goal of being present or mindful or whatever the goal is supposed to be. Just to look. To notice that a cup is a cup and a tree is a tree and that you're looking at it. Not as a meditation practice. Not as a productivity hack. Just as something you're doing.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote about "decreation"—the idea of stepping out of the way, of reducing yourself to nothing so that you could be genuinely receptive to reality. She thought most of our perception was actually us projecting our preconceptions onto the world, not actually seeing the world at all. To really see, we'd have to get ourselves out of the way somehow.

I think she was right, but I also think it's impossible. You can never fully get yourself out of the way. You're always there, looking through your own perspective, filtered through your own experiences and assumptions. The best you can do is maybe notice that you're doing it. Notice that you're seeing the world through yourself. And then try, gently, to see around yourself when you can.

---

There's been a lot of discourse lately about how everyone is depressed and anxious. The statistics support this—rates of depression and anxiety disorders are higher than they used to be, at least by some measures. And I believe it, because I can feel it in the culture. There's this underlying hum of anxiety, a sense that something is wrong and we're all complicit in the wrongness, and we don't know how to fix it so we just try not to think about it too hard.

I wonder sometimes if the anxiety is the problem, or if the anxiety is appropriate, and the problem is that we're not supposed to feel fine about things that aren't fine. Maybe some depression is rational. Maybe some anxiety is justified.

But then the trick is: how do you live in a state of awareness about real problems without completely immobilizing yourself? How do you care about things—climate change, inequality, suffering—without letting that care destroy you?

I don't have an answer. I suspect nobody does. I suspect everyone is just kind of muddling through, oscillating between awareness and dissociation, trying to find some balance that lets them exist without either fully denying reality or being completely crushed by it.

Sometimes I think the fact that we can care about things that don't directly affect us—that we can feel empathy for strangers, that we can mourn the destruction of ecosystems we'll never see—is one of the most beautiful things about being human. It's also kind of a curse. It means we can suffer in ways that animals probably don't, because we're aware of suffering that isn't happening to us directly, and we care anyway.

---

I've been thinking about forgetting. How we forget almost everything that happens to us. Every day, thousands of moments occur, and we experience exactly zero of them consciously, because most of what we do is automatic. And of the moments we do experience consciously, we forget almost all of them. A few decades later, you look back on your life and the only things you remember are maybe fifty or a hundred moments. All the rest has just dissolved into nothing.

This seems, on the face of it, tragic. All that life, gone. All those moments, wasted because nobody was paying attention.

But maybe that's not the right way to think about it. Maybe moments don't need to be remembered to have mattered. Maybe the fact that you lived them is enough. Maybe being alive is not about accumulating memories or experiences to look back on, but just about the actual living of it, the being of it.

The only person who was present for your breakfast this morning was you. You will probably forget it within a year. But someone saw your face while you were eating. You existed in that moment. Your consciousness was there. The moment happened. That seems like it should be enough.

Although I notice I still take photos of things. I still try to write down my thoughts. I'm still trying to preserve moments, to make them mean something by transforming them into data that can be stored and retrieved later. I'm not sure if that's wisdom or compulsion or some combination of both.

---

A friend of mine recently went through a really difficult breakup. We were talking about it, and they said something that stuck with me. They said that the hardest part wasn't the sadness, but the sense of wasted time. All those hours spent with a person, and now they feel like they don't count because the relationship ended. Like the only thing that matters is the outcome, and since the outcome was failure, all the time was wasted.

I think that's a very poisonous way to think about time, but I also think it's the way almost everyone thinks about time. We're trained to see time as an investment, and investments are only good if they have a good return. Time spent on things that don't lead anywhere is wasted time.

But what if that's backwards? What if time spent is time spent, regardless of where it leads? What if you can't waste time by living it, even if it doesn't lead anywhere?

I don't know. I'm clearly not good at this. I still believe, most of the time, that time should lead somewhere. I still feel anxious when I'm not being productive. I still feel like I should be working toward something.

But I'm trying to notice when I think that, and to check in with whether it's actually true. Whether I actually need to be working toward something, or if maybe I could just exist for a while, without any trajectory, without any particular goal, and see if that's okay.

It usually isn't okay, actually. It feels disorienting. It feels like I'm wasting time, or like I'm lazy, or like I'm not meeting some invisible standard that I'm supposed to be meeting. But the fact that it feels that way doesn't necessarily mean it's true. It might just mean I'm very well-trained.

---

I think the thing I'm trying to get at, in this rather meandering way, is that I don't know how to live and I don't think anyone does. We're all just kind of making it up as we go along, pretending like there's some instruction manual we're supposed to be following, when actually there isn't one. There's just this strange, chaotic, beautiful, tedious, overwhelming fact of being alive, and we have to decide, moment by moment, what to do with it.

And most of us choose distraction, which makes sense. The straight-on experience of being alive is kind of a lot. It's easier to look at your phone. It's easier to be busy. It's easier to have goals and plans and things to work toward, because at least then you have a direction, even if you're not sure it's the right one.

But sometimes, maybe, it's worth just looking at things. Just noticing them. The cup, the tree, the light, the time passing. Not to accomplish anything or become better or achieve presence or whatever. Just because they're there, and you're there, and that's strange and unlikely and worth looking at.
